content: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a condition diagnosed based on behavioral criteria. It is characterized by difficulties in social communication and the presence of restricted or repetitive behaviors, or both. The diagnosis is made using established classification systems. Since the publication of the DSM-5 in 2013, children are now diagnosed with ASD as a single category, rather than being assigned subclassifications such as autistic disorder, Asperger syndrome, or pervasive developmental disorder-not otherwise specified. Diagnostic tools for ASD have been developed using methods such as interviews with parents or caregivers, direct observation of the child, or a combination of both. The primary objective of this review was to determine which diagnostic tools, including updated versions, most accurately diagnose ASD in preschool-aged children when compared to the clinical judgment of a multidisciplinary team. The review also aimed to compare the diagnostic accuracy of specific tools, such as the Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule (ADOS), Autism Diagnostic Interview-Revised (ADI-R), Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS), Diagnostic Interview for Social and Communication Disorders (DISCO), Gilliam Autism Rating Scale (GARS), and Developmental, Dimensional, and Diagnostic Interview (3di). Specific questions included: which tool has the highest diagnostic accuracy, whether any single tool is sufficient for diagnosis, whether combinations of tools improve diagnostic accuracy, and whether combining an interview tool with a structured observation test reduces false positives and negatives compared to using either test alone. The review also sought to determine whether any diagnostic tool performs better for specific age subgroups within the preschool range. Sensitivity (the ability to correctly identify children with ASD) and specificity (the ability to correctly identify children without ASD) were the primary measures of diagnostic accuracy. Both measures are important, as there is often a trade-off between them. The review included studies that reported diagnostic accuracy for the six tools mentioned above, involved preschool-aged children suspected of having ASD, and used a multidisciplinary assessment as the reference standard. Eligible study designs included cohort, cross-sectional, randomized test accuracy, and case-control studies. Data were collected and analyzed by two independent reviewers, with disagreements resolved by a third reviewer. Methodological quality was assessed using the QUADAS-2 instrument. The review included 21 analyses from 13 publications, many of which had a high risk of bias or potential conflicts of interest. The overall prevalence of ASD in the included studies was 74%. For ADOS, 12 analyses involving 1,625 children were included. Sensitivity for ADOS ranged from 0.76 to 0.98, and specificity ranged from 0.20 to 1.00. The summary sensitivity was 0.94 (95% CI: 0.89–0.97), and the summary specificity was 0.80 (95% CI: 0.68–0.88). For CARS, four analyses involving 641 children were included. Sensitivity for CARS ranged from 0.66 to 0.89, and specificity ranged from 0.21 to 1.00. The summary sensitivity was 0.80 (95% CI: 0.61–0.91), and the summary specificity was 0.88 (95% CI: 0.64–0.96). For ADI-R, five analyses involving 634 children were included. Sensitivity for ADI-R ranged from 0.19 to 0.75, and specificity ranged from 0.63 to 1.00. The summary sensitivity was 0.52 (95% CI: 0.32–0.71), and the summary specificity was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.61–0.95). Comparative studies were limited and too small to draw definitive conclusions. In two studies comparing ADI-R and ADOS, both tests had similar sensitivity, but ADOS had higher specificity. In two studies comparing ADI-R, ADOS, and CARS, ADOS had the highest sensitivity, while CARS had the highest specificity. One study examined the combined use of ADOS and ADI-R but found that combining the two did not improve sensitivity or specificity compared to using ADOS alone. The performance of all tools was lower when studies with a high risk of bias were excluded. The authors concluded that there is significant variability in the sensitivity and specificity of all diagnostic tools, likely due to methodological differences and variations in the clinical characteristics of the populations studied. Among the tools, ADOS was the most sensitive, while all tools performed similarly in terms of specificity. In populations with lower ASD prevalence, the risk of false positives (incorrectly identifying children without ASD as having ASD) would be higher. New versions of diagnostic tools are now available, but their accuracy needs to be assessed in clinically relevant settings, with low-risk methodologies, and in children with diverse abilities.
